lesson.title: f''(x): Prime Notation, One Derivative Further
lesson.summary: f''(x), read f double prime of x, is the Lagrange-notation name for the second derivative, and it extends naturally to f'''(x) and beyond as you keep differentiating.
lesson.body:
You already know f'(x) as the derivative of f. The second derivative is just the derivative of f'(x), and Lagrange notation names it by adding a second prime mark: f''(x) = (f')'(x). Each extra prime mark literally counts how many times you've differentiated the original function. It's a compact bookkeeping system: no new symbols to learn, just one more tick mark per differentiation.

You already saw where this leads: three prime marks give the third derivative, f'''(x). Beyond that, piling on more prime marks becomes hard to read at a glance, so the convention switches to a parenthesized superscript: f^(4)(x), f^(5)(x), and in general f^(n)(x) for the nth derivative. The parentheses are essential, since f^4(x) without them would normally mean f(x) raised to the fourth power, an entirely different thing.

Let f(x) = sin(x). Differentiating once gives f'(x) = cos(x). Differentiating a second time gives f''(x) = -sin(x). To evaluate the second derivative at a specific point, plug into this new function: f''(pi/2) = -sin(pi/2) = -1, and f''(0) = -sin(0) = 0. Each of these numbers tells you the concavity of the sine curve at that particular x-value: negative concavity at x = pi/2 (the curve bends downward there), and zero concavity exactly at x = 0, an inflection point.

A double prime never means squaring. f''(x) is not [f(x)]^2, and it is not [f'(x)]^2 either; it denotes differentiating twice, full stop. Keeping this straight matters because the next chapter introduces d^2y/dx^2, the Leibniz-notation version of the exact same quantity, whose numerator and denominator have their own superscript-2's that are just as easy to misread as literal squaring.
